questions.q: How many distinct tradeoffs from earlier in this course does this case study identify within the single Service Console scenario?
options: At least three -- performance vs. complexity, declarative vs. programmatic, and governance vs. agility
Exactly one -- performance vs. complexity only
Five, including build vs. buy and real-time vs. batch
None -- the scenario is purely a performance problem
questions.explain: The case study deliberately shows that a single real scenario can contain multiple simultaneous tradeoffs, and the skill being taught is recognizing all of them rather than stopping at the first one noticed.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say the console's slow page-load problem is a comparatively 'cheap' performance fix?
options: Because it requires no analysis at all

Because trimming unused related lists and simplifying the layout (possibly with Dynamic Forms) carries lower complexity risk than options like introducing a caching layer, so it's worth doing regardless of the other decisions
Because it eliminates the need to address the 60-element Flow
Because performance fixes never carry any complexity cost
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly distinguishes this low-risk fix from costlier performance interventions like caching, which is why it's recommended to ship first and independently of the harder Flow/Apex decision.

questions.q: What constraint from the scenario specifically shapes how the declarative-vs-programmatic tradeoff gets resolved for the 60-element Flow?
options: The company's budget is unlimited for this project
Salesforce no longer allows Flows with more than 50 elements

The team has no in-house developer, and leadership explicitly wants no new data-integrity incidents, which rules out both leaving the unmaintainable Flow as-is and a full rewrite the team can't safely build or maintain
Apex cannot be called from Flow under any circumstances
questions.explain: The resolution -- extracting one piece of complex sub-logic into a single, tested invocable Apex method called from a simplified Flow -- is shaped directly by the real constraint that there's no in-house developer and that data-integrity incidents are explicitly off the table.

questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend a lightweight governance path (peer review, sandbox pipeline with automated tests) rather than a formal change-advisory board for this 45-agent team's changes?
options: Because governance is unnecessary for any team under 50 people
Because peer review is faster than any form of automated testing
Because Salesforce prohibits change-advisory boards for Service Cloud

Because a heavy governance process would be mismatched to the actual risk of console and escalation-logic changes at this scale, which Lesson 14 identifies as the failure mode that produces workarounds
questions.explain: The case study applies Lesson 14's risk-tiering logic directly: a heavy board process for console tweaks at this team's scale would be governance mismatched to actual risk, which is exactly the mismatch that produces shadow-IT-style workarounds.

questions.q: Per this lesson, why is the lightweight governance fix deliberately tied to the timing of the Flow/Apex redesign rollout, rather than built on an independent timeline?
options: So the newly rebuilt automation doesn't immediately start accumulating the same kind of unreviewed tangle that caused the original problem
Because governance changes are always free and can be added at any time with no urgency
Because Salesforce requires governance changes to be deployed in the same release as any Apex change
Because the console performance fix depends technically on the governance change being in place first
questions.explain: The sequencing logic in this lesson ties the governance fix to the automation rebuild specifically so the new, cleaner implementation has a safer change path from day one, rather than repeating the original failure mode.
